# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

No Launch HN exists (HN search for Veles finds no launch thread: https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=Veles&tags=story).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

founder.order_why: The window question (screen 4) sits between two screens that carry the same kicker and the same question, so the context step is split in two around it instead of finishing before the window is asked, and screens 15 and 16 are labelled 'Interviews · sent' before anything has been sent.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 ask the same thing: 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks about sales leadership as a second role in the problem: my launch pitch is half about directors who can't see how reps negotiate and discount ('Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations'). The problem step also never asks about how long a new rep takes to learn the pricing (the 5 to 7 month ramp), which is my headline pain.

PRIMARY.order_why: The open question about how my last deal went with Sheets, slides, CRM and email comes last, after I've already been asked to pick what I'd most like made easier, so I'm choosing a pain point before I've been walked back through the actual deal that would remind me what hurt.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 1 and 2 both ask whether and how often I priced each enterprise deal, which feels like the same question twice with the second just counting weeks
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing about getting the price approved -- the wait on deal desk or my manager signing off on a discount, which is usually where a quote stalls for me for a day or two -- and nothing about how long it took to turn the quote around for the buyer.

screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach reps, but 'the Contacts page' is a Keel screen I have not seen in this flow, so the second option leans on something unexplained, and there is no way to combine named people with a posted link.
screens.why5: Nothing of the study's meaning changes here, and nothing of Veles's product or roles leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list of people Keel finds for me (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group I post one open link to (each person signs in with Google first)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is up top with '4 answered' beside it, but the line names only Frequency when three cards are short, and the '5 needed' that decides it only appears down on the cards.
screens.why_b2: The tally and 'bar 6 of 7' read cleanly, but I had to look twice to see why 7 people answered and only 4 count on three cards; the screen never says where the other 3 went.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my beliefs word for word, and Prevalence and Frequency carry the job line I confirmed, awkward as it reads in a sentence.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need more answers, but nothing tells me to send the study to more account executives or how many, or what the one held card means for Veles.
screens.why_b5: n is on every card, the short cards are called too few rather than guessed, and Prevalence at exactly 6 of 7 is called 'holding up', not strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of the 7 who answered counted on Frequency, Importance and Current solution (the other 3 did not quote in the window) and 5 are needed, so send the study to 2 or 3 more account executives; Prevalence holds at 6 of 7, right on the bar.

screens.why_b1: The status word "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for, 1 against, out of 7, with the marker at 6 and an axis from 0 to 7, so what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence is not one of the two beliefs I checked, and the line pastes my job field into a template, so it reads as "priced on approved terms" rather than what I mean, "had a buyer ask for a quote that had to be priced and approved". It is recognisable, but it is not my words.
screens.why_b4: "How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards" points me onward but says nothing about what clearing the bar exactly means for Veles, for example that the occasion is common enough to build on.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said outright, and "at your bar exactly" does not dress the result up as strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 had a buyer ask for a quote that had to be priced and approved in the last 4 weeks, exactly your 8 in 10 with only 7 people, so the occasion looks common but one more 'no' would sink it; check Frequency and Importance before leaning on it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, 4 counted against 5 needed, and the So line repeats it, so I know why there is no verdict.
screens.why_b2: The weeks axis and the middle answer of 3 read at once, but 'your bar · 3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)' uses the same '4' as 'weeks out of 4', and the legend 'at what you said / short of it' takes a second look before I see it means 3 of the 4 people counted.
screens.why_b3: I recognise my 2-to-4-weeks rhythm, but my job phrase is pasted into the frequency line and the question, so it asks 'in how many weeks did you price each enterprise deal?', which no AE would say; I meant weeks in which they quoted a deal.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer would settle it, or that all 4 counted so far sit inside my band.
screens.why_b5: n and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' are visible and nothing is overclaimed, but the status says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered · 4 counted', a small contradiction about who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted, 5 needed. All 4 quote a deal in 2 to 4 weeks out of 4 (middle answer 3 weeks), so one more clear answer would settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted, 5 needed', and the So line repeats it, so I know there is no call yet and why.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes the bars clear (4 people, two picks each, 8 picks) and the bar reads 3 of 4 people, but the strip under it shows 3 for and 5 against, which mixes picks with people, so I had to look twice to see that 5 'against' is not 5 account executives.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Importance' and the belief line are word for word what I checked, with 'Getting enterprise quotes priced and approved' named as my problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say I need one more counted rep, or that 3 of 4 leans my way but Mateo's 'price book is already in the CPQ' answer is the case to watch.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', but the verdict's '4 answered' conflicts with the count line's '6 answered · 4 counted', and the strip's 'against 5' could read as five people against me.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 reps counted put quoting in their two, which leans your way, but 5 are needed to call it; 2 of the 6 who answered weren't counted. Get one more rep's clear answer, and watch for teams like Mateo's whose CPQ already holds the price book.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted, 5 needed', and the So line repeats both, so I know why it is not called.
screens.why_b2: The answer bars and the 3 for, 1 against split read fast, but the headline says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered', and 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads as if my bar were 3 of 4 rather than 2 in 3 with 3 of 4 landing below, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Current solution' and the belief line match what I checked word for word, including my Sheets, slides, CRM and email-chains wording.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me one more counted account executive would let this be called, or that the lean so far is my way.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two uncounted answers are named with reasons, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 3 of 4 from being sold as a held belief.
screens.instead: Leaning your way, 3 of 4 counted said today's pricing fell short (only Mateo's CPQ setup didn't), but that's 4 counted of 6 answered, one short of the 5 needed; get one more account executive's last deal to call it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' beside it, but Importance is the only line shown -- Current solution, also too few to call, has no box at all, and nothing says whether its people gave no why or were never asked.
screens.why_b3: The Importance name and my belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next -- get more account executives to answer, or that one CPQ-equipped rep hints my segment should exclude teams already on a CPQ; I have to infer it.
screens.why_b5: It keeps to the one person who answered: '1 against · 1 asked their why here' and 'On their own (1)' make the tiny n plain, and nothing is generalised.
screens.why_b6: Mateo's quote adds something I did not type: where the price book already lives in a CPQ, quoting takes minutes and pipeline and forecast hygiene take the week, which tells me who is not my buyer.
screens.instead: Importance: too few to call (4 of 5 needed); the one rep against already quotes from a CPQ in minutes -- worth checking whether teams with a CPQ belong in the segment; Current solution: too few to call, no whys yet.

screens.why1: Opening by checking whether I've actually priced an enterprise deal recently is the obvious first thing to ask me before the story question.
screens.why2: The question folds two things together, pricing a deal and doing it on terms the company stands behind, and 'each' makes me wonder whether one deal that went over discount policy makes it a no.
screens.why3: Pricing and quoting enterprise deals in the last month is exactly what I do, so I can answer it from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but a gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, 'I'd rather not say' isn't an allowed chip, and 'I can't recall one particular deal' doesn't fit a yes-or-no about the last four weeks.
screens.why5: The stem is the founder's job line pasted in word for word, and 'terms the company stands behind' is their phrase, not how a rep talks about getting a quote approved.
screens.why6: It is one question ending in 'Yes or no', but 'on terms the company stands behind' is a clause I'd have to hold and puzzle over when I hear it.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, did you price and quote an enterprise deal for a buyer? Yes · No

screens.why1: After asking whether I priced deals in the last four weeks, asking how often follows naturally.
screens.why2: "Price each enterprise deal" in "how many weeks did you price each enterprise deal" reads oddly; I'd say "in how many weeks did you work up pricing on a deal" and had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know which weeks I was building quotes and chasing approvals, so I can answer this from my own month.
screens.why4: 1 to 4 covers every week count for someone who already said yes, and "I can't recall" is a fair escape.
screens.why5: "Price each enterprise deal" is the founder's phrase lifted straight in; the "each" makes no sense counted per week, so it drifts from a person's real words.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and "a number from 1 to 4" is easy to hold when heard.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, in how many weeks did you work out pricing for an enterprise quote? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Having said how often I priced deals, asking which part of the deal grind I'd most like eased is the obvious next question and doesn't repeat anything.
screens.why2: Quotes, approval, pipeline, quota, procurement, CRM and forecast are my everyday words, though "last run of enterprise deals" is a slightly odd way to say my recent deals.
screens.why3: These are exactly the things I fought with on my last few deals, so I can pick one from memory without guessing.
screens.why4: The buyer's legal review and the buyer's procurement process often blur into one stage for me, since redlines usually come back through procurement, so those two overlap a little.
screens.why5: Getting quotes priced and approved is one honest option among five of my real headaches, with none of the founder's product or phrasing showing through.
screens.why6: One short question, then five parallel phrases I can hold and "none of these" said last; CRM is said aloud in my trade every day.
screens.instead: Think of your last few enterprise deals. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Getting quotes priced and approved; getting through the buyer's legal and procurement; keeping enough pipeline to hit quota; keeping the CRM and forecast current; or getting the buyer to a decision. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last deal actually went with the sheets, decks, CRM and email is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It says 'your last deal' but then 'pricing deals', and listing four tools in the middle of the question makes me read it twice to see it's just asking how my last quote went.
screens.why3: I priced a deal in the last few weeks with exactly that mess of spreadsheets and email, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: Each option packs two things together (how fast the pricing went and how the approval went), and the first two overlap, since a quick build with one approval fits both; there's also no clean 'built fine but waited days on approval'.
screens.why5: Sheets, slides, manual CRM entries and email chains are my own words for how we do it, and nothing about anyone's product reaches me.
screens.why6: Hearing the four-tool list inside the question and then five options that each have two comma clauses is a lot to hold in one listen.
screens.instead: Think of your last deal. How did getting its price worked out and approved go? Built quickly, approved first time; built quickly, waited on approval; slow to build, approved first time; slow to build and slow to approve; or terms changed after the quote went out. Or say you can't recall.
